title: Snakes and Ladders: The Quickest Way Up
directAnswer: Model the 100 squares as graph nodes. From any square you roll 1–6, so each square has up to six outgoing edges; if a destination square is the foot of a ladder or the mouth of a snake, you are immediately moved to its other end. Every roll costs one move, so BFS from square 1 gives the fewest rolls to reach square 100. The board is fixed at 100 squares, so it runs in O(1).

remember.pattern: BFS over an implicit board graph; apply jumps when landing
rules: Each roll is **one** move regardless of whether you advance 1 or 6 — so all edges weigh the same and BFS is exact.
Apply the snake/ladder jump to the **landing** square, not to the square you rolled from.
A landing square that is a snake/ladder mouth has **no separate visit** — you go straight to its end; mark the end visited.
Ignore rolls that overshoot 100 (`u + roll > 100`); you can only finish by landing exactly or being carried by a ladder.
Return `-1` if square 100 is never reached — snakes can trap some boards.
whenToUse: Shortest number of moves on a board / grid where each move has the same cost
The graph is **implicit** — edges come from rules (dice rolls), not an edge list
Teleports / portals that relocate you on arrival (ladders, snakes, warps)
Fixed, small state space where BFS explores everything once
antiSignals: Moves have differing costs → Dijkstra, not BFS
You need the count of distinct paths, not the shortest → DP over the DAG
The board is enormous and structured → look for a closed-form or math shortcut
You must maximize score along the way → this is an optimization DP, not pure shortest path
remember.takeaway: Snakes and Ladders is shortest-path in disguise: squares are nodes, dice rolls are equal-weight edges, and ladders/snakes are 'apply on arrival' redirects. Recognizing the implicit graph turns a board game into a textbook BFS.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can model a rules-based board as an implicit graph, see that equal-cost moves call for BFS, and correctly apply jumps to the landing square rather than double-counting them as extra moves.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Treating a ladder/snake as a separate move (it is free — part of landing), or applying the jump to the current square instead of the destination, or marking the mouth visited instead of the end.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Build a jump[] lookup so the snake/ladder remap is O(1), state that a roll is always one move so BFS (not Dijkstra) is right, and handle the overshoot and -1 cases explicitly.

problemStatement:
You play on a board of squares numbered `1` to `100`. You start on square `1`. On each turn you roll a die and advance `1` to `6` squares. Some squares are connected by **ladders** (climb up: landing on the foot moves you to the top) and **snakes** (slide down: landing on the mouth moves you to the tail).

Given the ladders and snakes, return the **minimum number of dice rolls** to reach square `100` from square `1`, or `-1` if it cannot be reached.
constraints: The board always has exactly 100 squares
0 ≤ ladders.length, snakes.length (each is a [start, end] pair)
Ladder start < ladder end; snake start > snake end
No square is the start of more than one snake or ladder
Squares 1 and 100 are never a snake or ladder endpoint that conflicts with the rules
understanding: Think of each of the 100 squares as a node. A single die roll takes you from square `u` to one of `u+1 … u+6`. If the square you land on is the foot of a ladder or the mouth of a snake, you are immediately and freely relocated to its other end — that relocation is part of the same move, not an extra one. Because every move (one roll) costs the same, the minimum number of rolls is the shortest path in this graph, which BFS computes by exploring squares in increasing roll count.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a ladder or snake an extra move?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it is applied automatically when you land. One roll = one move, even if it ends with a long climb or slide.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have to land on 100 exactly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You finish when you reach 100, either by landing on it or by a ladder carrying you there. A roll that would pass 100 is simply not taken.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a ladder's top itself be the foot of another ladder (chained jumps)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By the constraints each square starts at most one snake or ladder, so jumps do not chain. I will model jump[] as a single hop per square.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is 100 always reachable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily — a board of snakes can trap you. If BFS never marks square 100, return -1.

examples.explanation: Roll 5 (1→6), roll 6 (6→12, ladder to 98), roll 2 (98→100). Three rolls reach the top.
Roll 3 from square 1 lands on square 4, whose ladder carries you straight to 100 — one roll.
No jumps: advancing 99 squares at 6 per roll needs ⌈99/6⌉ = 17 rolls.

approaches.name: Recursive Move Search (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the literal 'try every dice sequence' idea — then show why snakes make it loop and motivate BFS with a visited set.

complexity.time: Exponential without memo / unsafe with cycles

hints: The brute-force instinct: from a square, try all six rolls, recurse, and take 1 + the minimum of the results.
Now add a snake that sends square 20 back to square 5. What happens when your recursion goes 5 → 20 → 5 → 20 …?
Cycles mean plain recursion never terminates. You would need a visited guard — and once you add that, a queue (BFS) is the cleaner shape.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Without memoization the recursion branches by 6 at each square — exponential. Memoization fails outright because snakes create cycles, so 'minimum rolls from square s' depends on itself. Bolting on a visited set turns it into a clumsy DFS that does not give shortest paths reliably.
approaches.explanation:
The natural first idea is to treat 'minimum rolls from square `s`' as a recursive quantity: try each of the six rolls, recurse on where you land (after any jump), and return `1 + min` over the six.

**Why memoized recursion does not work here.** Memoization assumes the dependency graph of subproblems is a DAG — that `f(s)` depends only on strictly 'smaller' states. Ladders and snakes break that. A snake from `20 → 5` means reaching `20` lets you go back to `5`, so `f(5)` depends on `f(20)` which depends on `f(5)`. The recursion has a *cycle*, and there is no base ordering to memoize against.

**Why even a visited-guarded DFS is wrong for this question.** You can stop infinite loops by refusing to revisit a square within the current path, but DFS explores depth-first, so the first time it reaches square 100 is not necessarily by the fewest rolls. You would have to explore *all* paths and take the minimum — exponential again.

**The lesson it teaches.** The cycles plus the 'fewest moves' objective are exactly the signature of a shortest-path problem on a graph with cycles. The right tool processes squares in increasing distance and marks each visited once — that is BFS. Use this baseline to explain *why* you abandon recursion, not as something you would submit.
approaches.insight: Snakes turn the state dependency into a cycle, which is precisely what kills naive recursion/DP. The moment you reach for a visited set to break the cycle, you have rediscovered BFS — so go there directly.

dryRun.intro: Trace the recursion to expose the cycle that makes it loop forever.

code.python:
# Illustrative only — loops on boards with snakes.
def min_rolls(self, square: int, jump: list[int], in_path: set[int]) -> int:
    if square == 100:
        return 0
    in_path.add(square)
    best = float('inf')
    for roll in range(1, 7):
        nxt = square + roll
        if nxt > 100:
            break
        nxt = jump[nxt]                     # apply ladder/snake on landing
        if nxt not in in_path:              # crude cycle guard
            sub = self.min_rolls(nxt, jump, in_path)
            if sub != float('inf'):
                best = min(best, 1 + sub)
    in_path.discard(square)
    return best                             # explores all paths → exponential

java.line: next = jump[next];                 // apply ladder/snake on landing
java.explanation: The jump is part of landing — applied to the destination, not the source square.
Needed only because snakes create cycles — the symptom that this should be BFS.

java.line: return best;                            // explores all paths → exponential
java.explanation: Taking min over all paths is exponential; DFS order does not give shortest first.

python.line: nxt = jump[nxt]                     # apply ladder/snake on landing
python.explanation: Remap the landing square through the jump table.

python.line: if nxt not in in_path:              # crude cycle guard
python.explanation: Blocks the 5→20→5 loop a snake would otherwise cause.

python.line: return best                             # explores all paths → exponential
python.explanation: Correctness requires exploring every path — far too slow; BFS fixes both issues.

pitfalls: Trying to memoize across a cycle — there is no valid subproblem ordering.
Assuming DFS finds the shortest path — it does not visit in distance order.
Applying the jump to the current square instead of the landing square.

approaches.name: BFS over the Board Graph (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer. Build a jump[] table, BFS from square 1, and the level at which square 100 is first reached is the minimum number of rolls.
hints: Each square is a node; a single roll is an edge to one of the next six squares (after any jump). Every edge costs one move.
Precompute jump[s] = the snake/ladder end if s starts one, else s itself. Then a move from u to u+roll lands on jump[u+roll].
BFS from square 1. The first time square 100 is dequeued (or marked), its distance is the minimum number of rolls. Use a visited array to handle the cycles snakes create.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The board is fixed at 100 squares, each with at most 6 outgoing edges, so BFS does at most 100 × 6 = 600 constant-time steps. With a fixed-size board that is O(1) time and space. (For a general N×N board it would be O(N²).)
approaches.explanation:
BFS is the exact fit: equal-cost moves, an implicit graph, and cycles handled by a visited set.

**Modeling the board as a graph.** Each square `1…100` is a node. From square `u`, a die roll of `r ∈ {1,…,6}` moves you to `u + r`. If `u + r` is the foot of a ladder or the mouth of a snake, you are carried to its other end. Precomputing `jump[s]` — the endpoint if `s` starts a snake/ladder, otherwise `s` — makes that redirect an `O(1)` lookup. So the real neighbor of `u` for roll `r` is `jump[u + r]`.

**Why a roll is one edge, not the distance you travel.** Whether you advance one square or six, or then climb a long ladder, it all happens in a single turn. So every edge in this graph has weight one. With uniform weights, BFS visits squares in increasing number of rolls, and the first time it reaches square 100 is by the fewest rolls — no priority queue needed.

**Why the visited set is essential.** Snakes send you backward, creating cycles. Without a visited marker, BFS could enqueue the same square endlessly. Marking each square the first time it is reached (its shortest-roll distance) both guarantees termination and keeps the work `O(board)`.

**Why the loop is iterative.** BFS runs off a FIFO queue with no recursion, so there is no call-stack depth to worry about — the cycle-laden board cannot overflow the stack the way the recursive baseline threatened to.

**Handling overshoot and unreachable.** A roll with `u + r > 100` cannot be played, so skip it. If the queue empties without ever marking square 100, the goal is unreachable on this board and the answer is `-1`.
approaches.insight: The whole problem collapses once you see squares as nodes and rolls as equal-weight edges, with `jump[]` folding each snake/ladder into an O(1) 'apply on arrival' redirect. BFS then reads off the answer as the level of square 100.

pitfalls: Counting a ladder or snake as an extra move — it is free, part of landing.
Applying the jump to the source square instead of the landing square.
Marking the snake/ladder mouth visited instead of its endpoint, so the real target is re-enqueued.

commonMistakes: Treating a ladder or snake as a separate move instead of a free relocation on landing.
Applying the jump to the current square rather than the destination of the roll.
Using DFS or Dijkstra when uniform-cost BFS is both correct and simplest.
Omitting the visited set, so snakes cause the BFS queue to cycle forever.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting the jump as an extra roll
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A ladder or snake fires automatically when you land — it does not consume a turn. Adding 1 for the jump inflates the answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
nxt = u + roll
d = dist[u] + 1
if jump[nxt] != nxt:
    d += 1            # wrong: the jump is free
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
nxt = jump[u + roll]   # land + jump, all one move
d = dist[u] + 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Jumping from the wrong square
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Snakes and ladders act on the square you LAND on, not the square you roll from. Remapping u before adding the roll skips the actual rule.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int from = jump[u];          // wrong: remap source
int next = from + roll;
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int next = jump[u + roll];   // remap the landing square

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the visited guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A snake sends you backward, so without marking squares visited the same square is enqueued repeatedly and BFS never terminates.

patternNote: BFS over an Implicit Board Graph. Recognize it when moves cost the same and the graph is described by rules (dice rolls, neighbor steps) with 'apply on arrival' redirects like ladders or portals. A jump[] table makes the redirect O(1); BFS reads off the fewest moves. The same shape powers Word Ladder, Open the Lock, and grid shortest paths.
